questions.prompt: In the systemic circulation, the veins serve as capacitance vessels and contain more than 60% of the total blood volume at rest.
The linear velocity of blood flow is highest in the aorta because it possesses the smallest total cross-sectional area of any segment in the vasculature.
The first heart sound (S_1) is produced by the closure of the atrioventricular valves at the beginning of the isovolumetric contraction phase.
In a normal SA node action potential, the upstroke of Phase 0 is primarily driven by a rapid inward sodium current (I_Na).
The T wave of a standard electrocardiogram represents the repolarization of the ventricles.
Conduction velocity through the myocardium is fastest in the atrioventricular (AV) node to ensure a delay that permits adequate ventricular filling.
The P-R interval on an ECG represents the total time from the initial depolarization of the atria to the initial depolarization of the ventricles.
The absolute refractory period in cardiac ventricular muscle corresponds approximately to the duration of the action potential plateau.
The "funny" current (I_f) is an inward sodium current responsible for the spontaneous phase 4 depolarization in the sinoatrial node.
The third heart sound (S_3) is a normal physiological finding in healthy children and is caused by rapid ventricular filling during early diastole.
The pulmonary artery carries blood that typically has the lowest partial pressure of oxygen (P_O2) in the systemic circuit.
The Purkinje system has the fastest conduction velocity of all cardiac tissues, whereas the AV node has the fastest intrinsic pacemaker rate.
The dicrotic notch (incisura) on an aortic pressure trace is generated by the sudden opening of the aortic valve during rapid ejection.
The QRS complex on an ECG represents the repolarization of the atria, which is normally masked by ventricular activity.
Gap junctions at the intercalated disks are the low-resistance pathways that allow the heart to function as an electrical syncytium.
The ejection fraction is defined as the volume of blood remaining in the ventricle after systole divided by the end-diastolic volume.
Capillary walls are relatively impermeable to lipid-soluble gases like O_2 and CO_2 , requiring them to cross via water-filled clefts.
According to Poiseuille's equation, if the radius of a vessel decreases by 50%, the resistance to blood flow through that vessel increases by a factor of 16.
Mean arterial pressure is weighted more heavily toward diastolic pressure because a greater fraction of the cardiac cycle is spent in diastole than in systole.
Arterioles are considered the primary resistance vessels because they exhibit the largest pressure drop across any segment of the systemic vasculature.
Compliance is a measure of the distensibility of a vessel and is defined mathematically as the change in pressure per unit change in volume.
The Frank-Starling law of the heart states that the force of ventricular contraction is a function of the initial fiber length, or preload.
Atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP) is released in response to high atrial pressure and acts to increase renal sodium reabsorption to expand blood volume.
Myogenic autoregulation of blood flow occurs when vascular smooth muscle contracts in response to being stretched by increased perfusion pressure.
Capillary hydrostatic pressure (P_c) is generally higher at the arteriolar end than at the venous end of a capillary bed.
Laminar blood flow is characterized by a parabolic velocity profile where velocity is highest at the center of the vessel.
The major form of CO_2 transport in systemic venous blood is dissolved CO_2 gas in the plasma.
Mean systemic filling pressure is a measure of the "fullness" of the vascular system and increases as venous compliance decreases.
Total peripheral resistance (TPR) is the primary determinant of the slope of the cardiac function curve.
In a closed circulatory loop, blood flow through the aorta must equal the sum of blood flow through all systemic capillaries.
The law of Laplace for a sphere explains why a dilated heart must develop greater wall tension to generate the same systolic pressure as a normal-sized heart.
The equilibrium operating point of the cardiovascular system is the intersection of the cardiac function and vascular function curves.
In a patient with iron-deficiency anemia, Reynolds number increases because the decrease in hematocrit reduces blood viscosity.
Cardiac glycosides like digitalis produce a positive inotropic effect by inhibiting the Na^+-K^+ATPase, which indirectly increases intracellular Ca^(2+)  levels.
During strenuous exercise, total peripheral resistance increases because of the mass sympathetic discharge to all systemic arterioles.
Moving from a supine to a standing position causes a transient decrease in venous return and cardiac output, triggering the baroreceptor reflex.
Activation of the sympathetic nervous system during exercise increases heart rate by increasing the Na^+ current (I_f) in the SA node.
In a patient with hyperthyroidism, the pulse pressure is typically increased due to a simultaneous increase in stroke volume and decrease in arterial compliance.
Histamine promotes local edema by dilating arterioles and constricting venules, both of which increase capillary hydrostatic pressure.
During the Valsalva maneuver, the initial increase in intrathoracic pressure causes an immediate increase in venous return to the right atrium.
Propranolol decreases cardiac output by antagonizing β_1-adrenergic receptors in the heart, leading to negative chronotropic and inotropic effects.
A patient with a pheochromocytoma secreting mainly norepinephrine will typically present with warm, flushed skin due to β_2-mediated vasodilation.
In a left-to-right ventricular shunt, the output of the right ventricle is significantly higher than the output of the left ventricle.
Paradoxical splitting of the second heart sound occurs when the pulmonic valve closes before the aortic valve, often seen in left bundle branch block.
In a pressure-volume loop, an increase in afterload results in an increased end-systolic volume and a decreased stroke volume for that cycle.
A clockwise rotation of the vascular function curve indicates an increase in total peripheral resistance (TPR).
The Bainbridge reflex facilitates an increase in heart rate when the low-pressure atrial receptors detect an increase in blood volume.
If the SA node firing rate is suppressed by strong vagal stimulation, the bundle of His can assume the role of an ectopic pacemaker at a rate of 15-20 beats/min.
A positive dromotropic effect on the AV node results in a shortening of the P-R interval on the electrocardiogram.
In heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, the ventricles compensate by increasing end-diastolic volume, which decreases wall stress according to Laplace's Law.
